beats.intro: Chapter eight, lesson five. Enzymes and the activation energy barrier. [[cube]]A sugar cube sits on a table, in air full of oxygen. Burning it would release a lot of energy, yet it just sits there. It will not start on its own. [[cells]]But inside a living cell, sugars are broken down in a blink, at body temperature. [[strip]]Here is our metabolic pathway again. [[lit]]Today we light up enzyme one, and find out how it makes reactions fast.
beats.catalyst: [[cat]]A catalyst is a chemical agent that speeds up a reaction without being consumed by it. [[enz]]An enzyme is a catalytic protein. [[sucrose]]Take sucrose, table sugar: a glucose and a fructose joined together. [[split]]With water, it can be split apart. This is hydrolysis, and the enzyme sucrase carries it out. The bond between the two sugars breaks, water divides into H and O H, and one piece goes to each sugar. [[after]]And sucrase comes out unchanged, ready for the next sucrose. One enzyme molecule can do this again and again, which is why a cell needs only a little of it. Notice that sucrase is a protein, and it works on sucrose only. Every step of our pathway has its own enzyme.
beats.barrier: [[bonds]]Every reaction between molecules involves breaking old bonds and forming new ones. [[graph]]Draw it as a curve, with free energy going up, and the progress of the reaction going across. The reactants sit on the left. The products sit lower, on the right, so delta G is negative, and the reaction is downhill. [[hump]]But between them stands a hill. To get over it, the molecules must first strain their bonds into an unstable transition state. [[ea]]The energy needed to climb that hill is the free energy of activation, or simply, the activation energy. [[ball]]Think of a ball resting in a dip, behind a ridge. Beyond the ridge it rolls downhill, but first it needs a push. A reaction can be downhill overall, and still be stuck at the bottom of that dip. That is why a downhill reaction is not always a fast one.
beats.heat: [[heat]]Where does the push come from? Often from heat. The reactant molecules absorb thermal energy from their surroundings, so they move faster and collide harder. [[cube2]]Heat the sugar cube enough, and it burns. A flame is a very large push. [[cell]]But a cell cannot do that. Heat strong enough to cross the barrier would damage its proteins, and it would speed up every reaction at once, wanted or not. [[need]]So the cell needs another way: make the hill lower.
beats.q1: Quick check. What is activation energy?
beats.lower: [[curve]]Enzymes catalyze reactions by lowering the activation energy barrier. [[two]]Here is the same reaction with an enzyme. The hill is lower, so at body temperature many more molecules have enough energy to cross it. [[dg]]Now look at the start and the finish. They did not move. Delta G is unaffected by the enzyme. [[only]]An enzyme cannot make an uphill reaction go. It only hastens reactions that would occur eventually. It is the same road, with a lower pass. And because an enzyme is not consumed, a single molecule can lower the barrier for one reaction after another. [[ex2]]Here is an everyday case. Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen on its own, but very slowly. [[cat2]]Add catalase, an enzyme found in a slice of raw potato, and the same reaction fizzes at once. The products are the same, and so is delta G. Only the speed has changed, because the hill is lower.
beats.q2: Quick check. What does the enzyme change?
beats.example: Let's try numbers. This is an example, not from the slides. [[no]]Say a reaction must climb twenty kilocalories per mole without an enzyme. [[yes]]An enzyme lowers the climb to eight. That is twelve less. [[same]]And if the reaction releases five kilocalories per mole, it still releases exactly five, with or without the enzyme. [[fast]]So the products form much faster, and the energy balance is the same. Notice what moved: only the top of the hill. The reactants and the products stayed exactly where they were.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up. An enzyme is a catalytic protein. [[s2]]Every reaction must first climb the activation energy barrier, and heat can supply that energy, but a cell cannot just heat up. [[s3]]Enzymes lower the barrier, and leave delta G alone. [[end]]Now try the practice.
